chapterNote: A song from a cave — Adullam or En-gedi, David hiding from Saul with the king's army in the valley below (1 Samuel 22, 24). It is a miktam, a 'golden' psalm, set to the tune 'Do Not Destroy,' and it moves from the shadow of God's wings to the dawn in eleven verses. The first half is the cave: be gracious, be gracious; my soul takes refuge under Your wings until the ruin blows over; I lie down among lions whose teeth are spears and whose tongues are sharp swords; they dug a pit in my path and fell into it themselves. The hinge is the refrain, sung twice, that lifts the psalm out of the cave entirely: be exalted, O God, above the heavens; let Your glory be over all the earth. And then the second half, which the church sings on Easter morning: my heart is steady, O God, my heart is steady; wake up, my glory; wake up, lute and lyre — I will wake the dawn. A man in a hole in the ground deciding to get up before the sun does, so that the sun finds him already singing. Verses 7-11 were later reused as the opening of Psalm 108.

1.text: For the choir director, to the tune 'Do Not Destroy.' A miktam of David, when he fled from Saul into the cave. Be gracious to me, O God, be gracious to me, for in You my soul takes refuge; in the shadow of Your wings I will shelter until the ruin has passed over.
1.amp: To the chief Musician [natsach], Altaschith ['Destroy not', Al-tashcheth, the KJV margin], Michtam [miktam — a golden poem] of David, when he fled [barach] from [panim] Saul [Shaul] in the cave [mearah]. Be merciful [chanan — be gracious] unto me, O God [Elohim], be merciful unto me: for my soul [nephesh] trusts [chasah — takes refuge] in You: yea, in the shadow [tsel] of Your wings [kanaph] will I make my refuge [chasah], until these calamities [havvah — ruin, destruction] be overpast [abar].
1.notes: The setting is 1 Samuel 22 or 24 — ba-mearah (H4631), in the cave — and the tune is al-tashchet (H516), 'do not destroy', David's own words when Abishai wanted to kill Saul in his sleep (cf. 1 Samuel 26:9). chonneni Elohim chonneni (H2603): grace asked twice, and chasah twice (H2620): be-tsel kenaphekha (H6738, H3671), under the wing-shadow, ad yaabor havvot (H5674, H1942) — until the ruin blows over like weather.

2.text: I cry out to God Most High, to God who brings it all to completion for me.
2.amp: I will cry [qara] unto God [Elohim] most high [Elyon]; unto God [El] that performs [gamar — completes, finishes] all things for me.
2.notes: eqra l-Elohim Elyon (H7121, H430, H5945): the Most High, from the bottom of a cave. la-El gomer alai (H410, H1584): the God who FINISHES for me — gamar is Psalm 138:8's verb, 'the LORD will complete what concerns me'. David does not know how; he knows Who.

3.text: He will send from heaven and save me; He puts to shame the one who tramples after me. Selah. God will send out His covenant love and His faithfulness.
3.amp: He shall send [shalach] from heaven [shamayim], and save [yasha] me from the reproach ['he reproacheth him that', charaph, the KJV margin] of him that would swallow me up [shaaph — pant after, trample]. Selah [selah]. God [Elohim] shall send forth [shalach] His mercy [chesed — covenant love] and His truth [emeth].
3.notes: yishlach mi-shamayim (H7971, H8064): help dispatched from above, as in Psalm 18:16. cheref shoaphi (H2778, H7602): the margin reads it as God shaming the panter — the enemy who breathes down David's neck. Then the two attributes sent like envoys: yishlach Elohim chasdo va-amitto (H430, H2617, H571) — covenant love and faithfulness as the rescue party.

4.text: My soul lies down among lions; I lie among men breathing fire — sons of men whose teeth are spears and arrows, and whose tongue is a sharp sword.
4.amp: My soul [nephesh] is among [tavek] lions [labi — lionesses, fierce lions]: and I lie [shakab] even among them that are set on fire [lahat — blazing], even the sons [ben] of men [adam], whose teeth [shen] are spears [chanith] and arrows [chets], and their tongue [lashon] a sharp [chad] sword [chereb].
4.notes: naphshi be-tokh lebaim (H5315, H8432, H3833): bedded down among lions — and the lions are bene adam (H1121, H120), men. lohatim (H3857): blazing, on fire with malice. The weapons are anatomical: shinnehem chanit ve-chitsim (H8127, H2595, H2671), u-leshonam chereb chaddah (H3956, H2719, H2299) — Saul's court ran on slander, and slander is a blade.

5.text: Be lifted high above the heavens, O God; let Your glory be over all the earth!
5.amp: Be You exalted [rum], O God [Elohim], above the heavens [shamayim]; let Your glory [kabod] be above all the earth [eretz].
5.notes: The refrain that lifts the psalm out of the cave: rumah al-ha-shamayim Elohim (H7311, H8064, H430) — be high above the sky — al kol-ha-aretz kebodekha (H776, H3519). A man in a hole prays for God's glory to fill the planet; the prayer is bigger than his predicament, which is how he survives it.

6.text: They set a net for my steps; my soul was bowed down. They dug a pit in front of me — and fell into the middle of it themselves. Selah.
6.amp: They have prepared [kun] a net [resheth] for my steps [paam]; my soul [nephesh] is bowed down [kaphaph]: they have digged [karah] a pit [shichah] before [panim] me, into the midst [tavek] whereof they are fallen [naphal] themselves. Selah.
6.notes: resheth hekhinu li-phamai (H7568, H3559, H6471): a net readied for his footsteps; kaphaph naphshi (H3721, H5315), the soul bent double. Then the reversal the Psalms love: karu le-phanai shichah, naphelu be-tokhah (H3738, H6440, H7882, H5307, H8432) — the pit-diggers in the pit, Saul's own spear coming back on him (cf. Psalm 7:15; Proverbs 26:27).

7.text: My heart is steady, O God, my heart is steady; I will sing, and I will make music.
7.amp: My heart [leb] is fixed ['prepared', kun — established, steadfast, the KJV margin], O God [Elohim], my heart is fixed: I will sing [shir] and give praise [zamar].
7.notes: nakhon libbi Elohim, nakhon libbi (H3559, H3820, H430): the same kun the enemies used to 'prepare' their net (v. 6) — now David's heart is the thing set firm. Said twice, because a heart in a cave has to be told twice. ashirah va-azammerah (H7891, H2167): the resolution to sing, before the rescue.

8.text: Wake up, my glory! Wake up, lute and lyre! I will wake the dawn itself.
8.amp: Awake up [ur — rouse yourself], my glory [kabod]; awake [ur], psaltery [nebel — lute] and harp [kinnor — lyre]: I myself will awake [ur] early [shachar — the dawn].
8.notes: urah khebodi (H5782, H3519): David rousing his own glory — his soul, his singing self — and urah ha-nebel ve-khinnor (H5035, H3658), the instruments told to get up. Then the line the church loves: airah shachar (H7837) — literally 'I will wake the dawn': not waiting for morning to bring hope but getting up first to sing it in. Easter's psalm.

9.text: I will give You thanks among the peoples, O Lord; I will make music to You among the nations.
9.amp: I will praise [yadah] You, O Lord [Adonai], among the people [am]: I will sing [zamar] unto You among the nations [leom].
9.notes: odekha ba-ammim Adonai (H3034, H5971, H136), azammerkha ba-leummim (H2167, H3816): thanksgiving with a Gentile audience — the cave-song already imagining a world stage, as Psalm 18:49 does. Paul heard the missionary note in these lines (cf. Romans 15:9).

10.text: For Your covenant love is vast — up to the heavens — and Your faithfulness reaches the clouds.
10.amp: For Your mercy [chesed — covenant love] is great [gadol] unto the heavens [shamayim], and Your truth [emeth] unto the clouds [shechaqim — the skies].
10.notes: ki-gadol ad-shamayim chasdekha (H1419, H8064, H2617): covenant love measured vertically, cave-floor to sky; ve-ad-shechaqim amittekha (H7834, H571), faithfulness to the cloud-layer. The two envoys of verse 3 turn out to be the size of the atmosphere.

11.text: Be lifted high above the heavens, O God; let Your glory be over all the earth!
11.amp: Be You exalted [rum], O God [Elohim], above the heavens [shamayim]: let Your glory [kabod] be above all the earth [eretz].
11.notes: The refrain of verse 5 word for word (H7311, H8064, H430, H3519, H776), now sung from the far side of the dawn. First it was a prayer against the lions; now it is the summary of the song. Psalm 108 opens with verses 7-11 of this psalm, spliced to Psalm 60 — the cave-song became a war-hymn.
